messages.subject: Re: Inactive data influencing analysis?
messages.subject_clean: Inactive data influencing analysis?
messages.body_plain:
Florian, (list)

Apologies for not getting to this earlier.  The basic problem here is
that you are trying to fit a 9 parameter model to 82 data points!  One
of your factor levels has only 1 observation, and another only 3.  It is
not surprising to me that you are getting strange results.  I do not
know enough about your study to suggest a more sensible alternative, but
with 82 observations AIC will undoubtedly select a model with far fewer
than 9 parameters.  Perhaps there is an ecologically meaningful
covariate that you could use that has a big effect on detectability but
that only has a few levels in the data, or that you could model as a
non-factor covariate.  An example of this (on a bigger dataset) is
observer in the paper on MCDS by Marques et al. (2007), at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/MarquesAuk2007.pdf

Now for the (less important) actual answer to your question:
Why did you get different results for two analyses that seem the same?
Actually, if you look closely at the data that is being output to the
MCDS engine, you will see that the order in which the observations are
output is different in the two analyses -- although all the same
observations are there.  The reason the order is different is to do with
the way that data are extracted from the distance project database using
database queries.  Normally the order of the data within transects does
not matter at all -- but in this case, because it's having trouble
converging in any case, it turns out that the order in which the
log-likelihoods are summed makes a tiny difference to the estimated
total log likelihood and is enough to convince it that it has not
converged.  As you probably know, floating point numbers cannot be
represented exactly on a computer and one consequence of this is that
the associative law only holds approximately for simple arithmetical
calculations.  I expect I could find a way to make these particular
computations more accurate, but it doesn't seem important given the
previous paragraph.  Also, interestingly, when I run the analyses on my
computer here, it gives the same answer for both projects (failure to
converge on both).

Hope this helps,

  - Len

--

messages.body_plain:
I would guess it is because you have rather spiked data (first histogram
bar higher than subsequent bars).  In this instance, the hazard-rate
model tends to fit the spike more closely, but because the spike
increases uncertainty, the variance goes up.  You need to decide whether
the spike is real, an artefact e.g. of rounding some distances to zero,
or due to small sample size fluctuation.  If it is real, you might give
some thought to trying to improve field methods to widen the shoulder of
the detection function.  If it is an artefact of rounding distance
estimates, then you should try to get more accurate estimates, e.g.
using a laser rangefinder.  If it is due to small sample size, then
ideally you would increase the size of your study (e.g. more transects
within your study area).

You're dealing with animals in groups or 'clusters'.  Another cause of a
spike in this circumstance is if the observer records the distance of
the nearest animals in a cluster to the line, instead of estimating the
location of the centre of the cluster, and measuring/estimating that
distance from the line.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Flavie:

The width of the confidence intervals around your point estimates are
measures of the precision in your estimates.  That overall uncertainty
is influenced by uncertainty in the 3 components in your density
estimate.  The components are
a) detection function,
b) encounter rate, and
c) (possibly) cluster size.

When you fit different detection functions to your distance data, you
are influencing the amount of uncertainty present in component (a).

You are correct that you will (almost) always have wider confidence
intervals from the hazard rate detection function than from the half
normal detection function fitted to the same set of observations.  This
is because the hazard rate function is more flexible (because it has 2
parameters) rather than a single parameter of the half normal function.

The cost of this added flexibility is that you are asking to estimate
twice the number of parameters from the same amount of data (number of
detections).  It stands to reason that you will be less certain about
the value of each parameter of the hazard rate function than you are
about the value of the shape parameter (sigma) of the half normal; given
the same amount of data.

Look at the coefficient of variation of the coefficients of the
respective detection functions; this will show you how uncertainty in
the parameters of the detection function is influenced by the number of
parameters in the detection function.  This propagates into the
uncertainty in p-hat (the proportion of the animals within your
truncation distance that you detect).

You should *not* use confidence interval widths (or other measures of
precision) as a model selection criterion.  Remember, you not only wish
to have precise estimates, but you would also like to retain a nominal
("95%") probability that the true density of your population lies within
your confidence bounds.  The danger of using the model with the smallest
confidence interval is that you will be producing a precise answer, but
one that does not have the true density within its confidence interval.

Hi Flavie, List,

Not having seen your data - which is not ideal - here is a possible=20
explanation for what you describe. The half-normal (HN) always has a=20
very similar shape (this is because it only has a scale parameter, so it=20
always looks like half of a bell shaped curve, thought the cosine=20
adjustments might change it slightly). On the other hand, 2 different =20
hazard rates (i.e. with different parameter values) might look quite=20
distinct (the hazard rate has a scale and a shape parameter). This means=20
that the hazard rate might look quite spiked if the data presents a=20
large number of observations close to the line. The fact that in your=20
example the HR estimate has a CI that is far longer in the upper tail=20
seems to imply that your data cannot guaranty that the HR parameters=20
take values such that the function is not (at least slightly) spiked.=20
You should try to understand why that spike might arise, looking back at=20
your data. If all seems fine nonetheless, you might want to use some=20
type of model averaging to account for model uncertainty in this case=20
(e.g. using the bootstrap and letting distance choose the key function=20
at each resample), rather than just using the lowest AIC model.

You should never choose a model on the basis that is gives you a smaller=20
CI - this usually just means you are overly confident about your=20
inferences than what you should be.

Hope this helps,

Tiago.

It is a rough guideline.  Accurate estimates of distances don't really
reduce the number needed, although if you can ensure that virtually all
animals are detected for some distance from the line, so that the
detection function has a wide 'shoulder', you can get away with fewer
detections and still have reliable estimation.  The software will work
on smaller sample sizes.  Whether you get a good estimate of density or
abundance with small samples depends on a range of factors, one of them
being luck.  e.g. if your detection function has a wide shoulder, but
your sample size is small, the histogram of detection distances may be
quite spiked (no shoulder) purely through chance, and then estimation
can be very unreliable.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Distance Sampling for flying seabirds
messages.subject_clean: Distance Sampling for flying seabirds
messages.body_plain:
We conduct at-sea surveys for pelagic seabirds in eastern Canadian
waters. At the recent Pacific Seabird Group meeting I had the
opportunity to discuss distance sampling for flying birds with other
North American pelagic surveyors.=20

A number of methods for dealing with flying birds are currently in use:

1. Count flying birds continuously, record distance at which bird was
first detected.
	- I asked about recording distances when birds are first
detected at the Distance workshop last year. I remember the consensus
was that this wasn't a good idea, but don't remember the details. Can
someone explain why or why not?
	- I think the continuous counting still overestimates flying
birds.

2. Tasker's "snapshot" method, no distance sampling
	- deals with overestimates due to continuous counting, but fails
to estimate detectability.

3. Tasker's "snapshot method", distances recorded at moment of snapshot
	- I think this will work fine and I'm really interested to hear
arguments either for or against it. =20

The Intro book (section 6.5.1, p. 202) recommends recording distances
when a flying bird comes abeam, regardless of when it was detected; OR a
slightly modified scheme (p. 203) where the "beam line" is projected
ahead of the ship, but still perpendicular to the transact. Both these
methods require constant tracking of flying birds to detect when they
cross the beam line, no matter where it is placed. Most observers felt
this method would divert attention away from the transect line,
resulting in loss of detections of birds on water at distance zero (i.e.
on the line) and it also may be quite onerous when it is busy.=20

The snapshot method in no. 3 above has the advantage that flying birds
can be ignored (if necessary during busy periods) until the moment of
the instantaneous snapshots.  At which point, all birds within the
snapshot box are counted and their distances recorded. A minor
disadvantage is that the observer still has to estimate whether the
birds are inside or outside the box, which I believe is no harder than
estimating when they cross a beam line projected ahead of the ship.

So, can anyone see anything about number 3 that drastically violates the
basic assumptions of Distance Sampling or suggest a better method?

Thanks for your help,
Dave
=20

Yes, it does.  This is because, if birds are flying, you preferentially
record them when they are relatively close to the line, as they are
easier to detect then.  Hence distances tend to be biased low, which

> > 	- I think this will work fine and I'm really interested to hear
> > arguments either for or against it.

This is akin to the snapshot method mentioned in the point transect
chapter of the 2001 book - see p147 and 173.  Yes, if you can record

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I like the discussed topics below; crucial for seabird monitoring and
management:

1.
if we assume that the box extent (as mentioned below) cannot really be
determined at sea (similar key argument than against plain strip transects),
the circular plot one (with correction for angle coverage) is the most
realistic solution, right ?

2.
I would be happy to read a protocol and paper that actually have used these
best methods above. Do we have some standard ones handy on either ?

3.
More specifically, which software and gadgets are used for achieving all
these goals (beyond note books and Cybertracker)?

4.
An add-on to the email below:
Flying birds in flocks: Using Flock Center for the distance I find rather
robust (most cases).

5.
Another add-on and rarely addressed:
Flight direction of birds. It affects density estimates. How would one deal
with it ?

6.
Having Metadata (FGDC NBII) on any of these things should be a must for us
by now.

7.
Overall, I assume we all agree that dealing with detectability in pelagic
Seabird Surveys is crucial, a best professional practice, and that sticking
to plain old strip transects is rather mis-leading and not appropriate in
the year 2008 and beyond for doing science-based monitoring and management
of seabirds and oceans, right ?
If so, then I think no (public) funding should be spent on things such as
plain strip transects anymore.

I would be very interested in feedback on these items.

Very best

Hi,

I like the discussed topics below; crucial for seabird monitoring and
management:

1.
if we assume that the box extent (as mentioned below) cannot really be
determined at sea (similar key argument than against plain strip transects),
the circular plot one (with correction for angle coverage) is the most
realistic solution, right ?

2.
I would be happy to read a protocol and paper that actually have used these
best methods above. Do we have some standard ones handy on either ?

3.
More specifically, which software and gadgets are used for achieving all
these goals (beyond note books and Cybertracker)?

4.
An add-on to the email below:
Flying birds in flocks: Using Flock Center for the distance I find rather
robust (most cases).

5.
Another add-on and rarely addressed:
Flight direction of birds. It affects density estimates. How would one deal
with it ?

6.
Having Metadata (FGDC NBII) on any of these things should be a must for us
by now.

7.
Overall, I assume we all agree that dealing with detectability in pelagic
Seabird Surveys is crucial, a best professional practice, and that sticking
to plain old strip transects is rather mis-leading and not appropriate in
the year 2008 and beyond for doing science-based monitoring and management
of seabirds and oceans, right ?
If so, then I think no (public) funding should be spent on things such as
plain strip transects anymore.

I would be very interested in feedback on these items.

Very best

Fifield,David [St. John's] wrote:
> > We conduct at-sea surveys for pelagic seabirds in eastern Canadian
> > waters. At the recent Pacific Seabird Group meeting I had the
> > opportunity to discuss distance sampling for flying birds with other
> > North American pelagic surveyors.
> >
> > A number of methods for dealing with flying birds are currently in use:
> >
> > 1. Count flying birds continuously, record distance at which bird was
> > first detected.
> > 	- I asked about recording distances when birds are first
> > detected at the Distance workshop last year. I remember the consensus
> > was that this wasn't a good idea, but don't remember the details. Can
> > someone explain why or why not?
> > 	- I think the continuous counting still overestimates flying
> > birds.
> >
Yes, it does.  This is because, if birds are flying, you preferentially
record them when they are relatively close to the line, as they are
easier to detect then.  Hence distances tend to be biased low, which
generates upward bias in the abundance estimate.
> > 2. Tasker's "snapshot" method, no distance sampling
> > 	- deals with overestimates due to continuous counting, but fails
> > to estimate detectability.
> >
Works fine if you can accurately assess where the box is, and can detect
all birds in the box.
> > 3. Tasker's "snapshot method", distances recorded at moment of snapshot
> > 	- I think this will work fine and I'm really interested to hear
> > arguments either for or against it.
This is akin to the snapshot method mentioned in the point transect
chapter of the 2001 book - see p147 and 173.  Yes, if you can record
distances from the line of each bird in flight at the snapshot moment,
this approach is fine.  It also works fine in a point transect
framework, where e.g. you record all visible birds in flight within a
sector ahead of the observer at the snapshot moment.
> >
> >
> > The Intro book (section 6.5.1, p. 202) recommends recording distances
> > when a flying bird comes abeam, regardless of when it was detected; OR a
> > slightly modified scheme (p. 203) where the "beam line" is projected
> > ahead of the ship, but still perpendicular to the transact. Both these
> > methods require constant tracking of flying birds to detect when they
> > cross the beam line, no matter where it is placed. Most observers felt
> > this method would divert attention away from the transect line,
> > resulting in loss of detections of birds on water at distance zero (i.e.
> > on the line) and it also may be quite onerous when it is busy.
> >
> > The snapshot method in no. 3 above has the advantage that flying birds
> > can be ignored (if necessary during busy periods) until the moment of
> > the instantaneous snapshots.  At which point, all birds within the
> > snapshot box are counted and their distances recorded. A minor
> > disadvantage is that the observer still has to estimate whether the
> > birds are inside or outside the box, which I believe is no harder than
> > estimating when they cross a beam line projected ahead of the ship.
> >
Might be better to have a circular plot, if you're able to record
distances at the snapshot moment (possibly in distance bands).  The plot
is then a circle or part-circle, centre located at the observer.  The
data would be analysed in the standard way for point transect sampling,
but if you have a sector with angle say 90 degrees, effort per point
would be 0.25 (90/360).

messages.body_plain:
Hi List,

I am engaged in setting up the analysis structure for a Distance project

in which the data will have to be analysed in 16 distinct geographic
parcels, for each of 4 species. I am wondering what approach to use to
keep the number of candidate models at manageable levels when
investigating different key functions, adjustments, and covariates.

My data are for bird sightings on farms over two years, and I would like

to try out a variety of promising covariates. The problem is that I see
the numbers of models ballooning enormously. If I were to assess all

possible combinations for a single species in a single area, I would get

(2 key functions [halfnormal, hazard]) * (3 adjustment terms [cos, sim,
her]) * (permutations of 6 covariates)
=3D 2048 models

Seeing that I would have to repeat THAT 64 times (for 4 species in 16

areas), this brute force approach obviously won't work. But I have a hard

time deciding where to simplify.
In my first attempt, I tried to find a good "base model" for each set,

just a key function + adjustment, without any covariates. Having selected

that, I then ran the 64 covariate permutations on this model, which is
manageable. But I've developed some doubt about the validity of this
approach. E.g., in the 2007 Auk paper by Marques et al. (Table 2), a
similar permutative approach suggests that in a ranking of models with

different key models, adjustment terms, and covariates, the same covariat=

e
combination with a different key model or adjustment choice can lead to

large AIC differences - meaning that having chosen a "base model" without
employing covariates, I can't be sure that for a given covariate, another

base model would not yield better results.

I suppose, although I am less sure, that a similar problem would occur if

I tried a stepwise addition of covariates instead of trialing all
combinations here. Having selected the best-performing covariate of the

1-covariate models and adding further covariates to this, I can't be sure

that a 2+ combination with another first covariate would not yield a

better fit. For some data sets, using full permutation, I have already ha=

d
results where the best model had covariates ABC and the second-best
covariate D only - meaning that starting from a "best single covariate"
base (D), I would never have found the best model.

I guess that one of these simplifying steps, or something similar, will b=
e
necessary though unless I want to run tens of thousands of models. I woul=
d
be very grateful for some guidance from those who have performed analyses

that were similarly in danger of inflation!

best regards
florian weller

Hi Florian, List,

I put forward the following ideas (others would naturally be possible)=20
to try to simplify your problem a bit:

(note: I'm missing how you got 2048 models below, as 2 key * 3=20
adjustments* 64 covariate combinations (which means no interaction terms=20
and all possibilities from no to 6 covariates) =3D384, and there is no=20
number which multiplied by it leads to 2048 - I might be missing=20
something rather obvious!)

1. There seems to be no way to simplify at the species level, so you=20
should need to deal with a separate analysis by species. Species could=20
be considered a covariate too, though there's probably no advantage in=20
doing so (unless sample size is small for some of the species - see=20
MATHEW W. ALLDREDGE, KENNETH H. POLLOCK, THEODORE R. SIMONS, SUSAN A.=20
SHRINER (2007) Multiple-species analysis of point count data: a more=20
parsimonious modelling framework Journal of Applied Ecology 44 (2) ,=20
281=96290 for details).

2. You might abstain from using all the combinations of key functions +=20
adjustment terms. Just try one of the adjustment terms (say cosine) and=20
then proceed. At the end you can do some exploratory EDA to see if=20
others would lead to substantial differences, I predict not. So you cut=20
the number of models to try by a factor of 3.

3. Try each covariate alone (with both key functions), and see if there=20
is some that look much more promising than others. Focus on those. It is=20
unlikely that after using the 2 our 3 that most help explaining the=20
detection function you still need the remaining 4 or 3. Also, it might=20
be the case that overall one of the key functions starts looking more=20
promising than the other. If that is not the case then you might need=20
some model averaging in the end. The advantage in the Auk paper you=20
refer was that despite having different AIC's, different models were all=20
leading to very similar density estimates, so the choice of model was=20
less influential in the final result.

4. Do you expect that detection probability will change by area? Is it=20
worth to include area as an additional covariate (say as a factor; it=20
depends on sample size if you actually can estimate all the parameters=20
involved), rather than treating it as a separate analysis by area?

Note the above is based on a pragmatic point of view. This is no=20
different than variable selection in the more general regression=20
context, and there are multiple strategies possible and problems=20
associated with each strategy under such a setting.

Hope this helps,

Tiago

Hi Dave,

I thought it would be worth adding my 10 pence to this, having used and
thought about the snapshot method (2 in your list of questions) extensive=
ly
over the years.

One of the main reasons that there has been such strong take-up of this
method is that it still works at very high encounter rates, which I fear
would not be the case if observers are asked to collect too much informat=
ion
at the time of the snapshot.

It is key to the snapshot method that it happens over as short a time fra=
me
as possible (Tony Gaston simulated the effect of extended snapshots in a
response to the Tasker et al. publication in The Auk (1987, 104:336-338))=
.=20
This is another reason for not trying to collect too much information at =
the
time of the snapshot count.

Measuring distances accurately at sea is problematic, so I would hazard
caution against trying to do anything too precise.  Also, one of the
assumptions of distance estimation is that animals are not reacting
(attracted to or repelled by) the observer or the observation base.  I th=
ink
that for some species, this is a significant problem, and a complex metho=
d
for estimating their abundance is giving you false precision.=20=20

I'm interested in Steve's suggestion of using a circular snapshot area
rather than a box-shape (I think a 90deg segment would be more practical)=
.=20
I would certainly expect it to be easier for observers than a box shape. =
 It
would be necessary to make adjustments to the way the snapshot method is
implemented, because the box-shaped snapshot simulates a complete strip
transect of 300 metres width for flying birds, and intervals between
snapshots are determined by the time it takes to travel the length of the=
 box.=20

I'd be very interested in hearing how you get on with any trials of optio=
n 3.

Best wishes

Andy
